claim: Efficient processing of sensory data requires adapting the neuronal encoding strategy to the statistics of natural stimuli.
source: Efficient processing of sensory data requires adapting the neuronal encoding strategy to the statistics of natural stimuli.
evidence: This is a general statement about efficient coding presented in the introduction without specific experimental data from this study.

claim: Local multipoint correlation patterns that are most variable in natural images are the most perceptually salient for human observers in a way compatible with the efficient coding principle.
source: Previously, in Hermundstad et al., 2014, we showed that local multipoint correlation patterns that are most variable in natural images are also the most perceptually salient for human observers, in a way that is compatible with the efficient coding principle.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Hermundstad et al., 2014).

claim: Four groups of rats were trained to discriminate between white noise patterns and binary textures containing variable intensity levels of one of four image statistics (from single- to four-point correlations).
source: Here we selected four image statistics (from single- to four-point correlations) and trained four groups of rats to discriminate between white noise patterns and binary textures containing variable intensity levels of one of such statistics.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and methods used in the current study.

claim: Rat sensitivity shows a sharp decrease from two- to four-point correlations and a further decrease from four- to three-point correlations.
source: We interpreted the resulting psychometric data with an ideal observer model, finding a sharp decrease in sensitivity from two- to four-point correlations and a further decrease from four- to three-point.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of psychometric data collected in the study using an ideal observer model.

claim: The sensitivity ranking observed in rats fully reproduces the trend previously observed in humans.
source: This ranking fully reproduces the trend we previously observed in humans, thus extending a direct demonstration of efficient coding to a species where neuronal and developmental processes can be interrogated and causally manipulated.
evidence: This claim compares the current rat data to previous human data from Hermundstad et al., 2014.

claim: The efficient coding principle has been successful in explaining many aspects of neural processing in vision, audition, and olfaction.
source: This normative principle, known as efficient coding, has been successful in explaining many aspects of neural processing in vision (Atick and Redlich, 1990; Fairhall et al., 2001; Laughlin, 1981; Olshausen and Field, 1996; Pitkow and Meister, 2012), audition (Carlson et al., 2012; Smith and Lewicki, 2006) and olfaction (Teşileanu et al., 2019), including adaptation (Młynarski and Hermundstad, 2021) and gain control (Schwartz and Simoncelli, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work in different sensory modalities.

claim: Human sensitivity to visual textures defined by local multipoint correlations depends on the variability of such correlations across natural scenes.
source: In Hermundstad et al., 2014, we reported that human sensitivity to visual textures defined by local multipoint correlations depends on the variability of such correlations across natural scenes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The allocation of resources to features that are most variable in the environment is accounted for by efficient coding.
source: This allocation of resources to features that are the most variable in the environment, and thus more informative about its state, is accounted for by efficient coding, demonstrating its role as an organizing principle also at the perceptual level (Hermundstad et al., 2014; Tesileanu et al., 2020; Tkacik et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: It remains unknown whether preferential encoding of texture statistics that are most variable across natural images is a general principle underlying visual perceptual sensitivity across species.
source: However, it remains unknown whether this preferential encoding of texture statistics that are the most variable across natural images is a general principle underlying visual perceptual sensitivity across species.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study aims to address.

claim: Evidence exists for differential neural encoding of multipoint correlations in macaque V2 and V1.
source: Although some evidence exists for differential neural encoding of multipoint correlations in macaque V2 (Yu et al., 2015) and V1 (Purpura et al., 1994), the sensitivity ranking we previously reported in Hermundstad et al., 2014 has not been investigated in any species other than humans (Hermundstad et al., 2014; Tesileanu et al., 2020; Tkacik et al., 2010; Victor and Conte, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neurophysiology studies in macaques.

claim: The sensitivity ranking reported in Hermundstad et al., 2014 has not been investigated in any species other than humans.
source: Although some evidence exists for differential neural encoding of multipoint correlations in macaque V2 (Yu et al., 2015) and V1 (Purpura et al., 1994), the sensitivity ranking we previously reported in Hermundstad et al., 2014 has not been investigated in any species other than humans (Hermundstad et al., 2014; Tesileanu et al., 2020; Tkacik et al., 2010; Victor and Conte, 2012).
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature based on review of previous studies.

claim: Rodents are more amenable than monkeys to causal manipulations such as optogenetic or controlled rearing experiments.
source: Moreover, while monkeys are standard models of advanced visual processing (DiCarlo et al., 2012; Kourtzi and Connor, 2011; Lehky and Tanaka, 2016; Nassi and Callaway, 2009; Orban, 2008), they are less amenable than rodents to causal manipulations (e.g. optogenetic or controlled rearing) to interrogate how neural circuits may adapt to natural image statistics.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge about experimental capabilities in different animal models.

claim: Rodents have emerged as powerful model systems to study visual functions during the last decade.
source: On the other hand, rodents have emerged as powerful model systems to study visual functions during the last decade (Glickfeld et al., 2014; Glickfeld and Olsen, 2017; Huberman and Niell, 2011; Katzner and Weigelt, 2013; Niell and Scanziani, 2021; Reinagel, 2015; Zoccolan, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to recent literature.

claim: Rats are able to employ complex shape processing strategies at the perceptual level.
source: Rats, in particular, are able to employ complex shape processing strategies at the perceptual level (Alemi-Neissi et al., 2013; De Keyser et al., 2015; Djurdjevic et al., 2018; Vermaercke and Op de Beeck, 2012), and rat lateral extrastriate cortex shares many defining features with the primate ventral stream (Kaliukhovich and Op de Beeck, 2018; Matteucci et al., 2019; Piasini et al., 2021; Tafazoli et al., 2017; Vermaercke et al., 2014; Vinken et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on rat visual processing.

claim: Rat lateral extrastriate cortex shares many defining features with the primate ventral stream.
source: Rats, in particular, are able to employ complex shape processing strategies at the perceptual level (Alemi-Neissi et al., 2013; De Keyser et al., 2015; Djurdjevic et al., 2018; Vermaercke and Op de Beeck, 2012), and rat lateral extrastriate cortex shares many defining features with the primate ventral stream (Kaliukhovich and Op de Beeck, 2018; Matteucci et al., 2019; Piasini et al., 2021; Tafazoli et al., 2017; Vermaercke et al., 2014; Vinken et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to comparative neuroanatomy studies.

claim: Rearing newborn rats in controlled visual environments allows causally testing hypotheses about the dependence of visual cortical development from natural scene statistics.
source: More importantly, it was recently shown that rearing newborn rats in controlled visual environments allows causally testing long-standing hypotheses about the dependence of visual cortical development from natural scene statistics (Matteucci and Zoccolan, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Establishing the existence of preferential encoding of less predictable statistics in rodents is crucial to understand the neural substrates of efficient coding and its relationship with postnatal visual experience.
source: Establishing the existence of a preferential encoding of less predictable statistics in rodents is therefore crucial to understand the neural substrates of efficient coding and its relationship with postnatal visual experience.
evidence: This is an inference about the importance of the current study based on the capabilities of rodent models.

claim: Rats were trained to discriminate binary textures containing structured noise from textures made of white noise.
source: To address this question, we measured rat sensitivity to visual textures defined by local multipoint correlations, training the animals to discriminate binary textures containing structured noise from textures made of white noise (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: White noise textures were generated by independently setting each pixel to black or white with equal probability, resulting in no spatial correlations.
source: The latter were generated by independently setting each pixel to black or white with equal probability, resulting in no spatial correlations.
evidence: This describes the method for generating control stimuli.

claim: Structured textures were designed to enable precise control over the type and intensity of the correlations they contained.
source: Structured textures, on the other hand, were designed to enable precise control over the type and intensity of the correlations they contained.
evidence: This describes the design of experimental stimuli.

claim: A software library was built and published that implements the method developed in Victor and Conte, 2012 for generating structured textures.
source: To generate these textures we built and published a software library (Piasini, 2021) that implements the method developed in Victor and Conte, 2012.
evidence: This describes a methodological contribution with citations to the original method and the new implementation.

claim: For any given type of multipoint correlation, textures were sampled from the distribution over binary textures that had the desired probability of occurrence of that statistic but otherwise contained the least amount of structure (maximum entropy).
source: Briefly, for any given type of multipoint correlation (also termed a statistic in what follows), we sampled from the distribution over binary textures that had the desired probability of occurrence of that statistic, but otherwise contained the least amount of structure (i.e. had maximum entropy).
evidence: This describes the method for generating textures based on Victor and Conte, 2012.

claim: The probability of occurrence of the pattern was parametrized by the intensity of the corresponding statistic, determined by a parity count of white or black pixels inside tiles of 1, 2, 3, or 4 pixels (termed gliders).
source: The probability of occurrence of the pattern was parametrized by the intensity of the corresponding statistic, determined by a parity count of white or black pixels inside tiles of 1, 2, 3, or 4 pixels (termed gliders) used as the building blocks of the texture (Victor and Conte, 2012).
evidence: This describes the parametrization method with citation to the original work.

claim: When the intensity is zero, the texture does not contain any structure and is the same as white noise.
source: When the intensity is zero, the texture does not contain any structure–it is the same as white noise (Figure 1A, left).
evidence: This describes a property of the stimulus generation method and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: When the intensity is +1, every possible placement of the glider across the texture contains an even number of white pixels.
source: When the intensity is +1, every possible placement of the glider across the texture contains an even number of white pixels, while a level of –1 corresponds to all placements containing an odd number of white pixels.
evidence: This describes a property of the stimulus generation method.

claim: When the intensity is -1, all placements of the glider contain an odd number of white pixels.
source: When the intensity is +1, every possible placement of the glider across the texture contains an even number of white pixels, while a level of –1 corresponds to all placements containing an odd number of white pixels.
evidence: This describes a property of the stimulus generation method.

claim: Intermediate intensity levels correspond to intermediate fractions of gliders containing the even parity count.
source: Intermediate intensity levels correspond to intermediate fractions of gliders containing the even parity count.
evidence: This describes a property of the stimulus generation method.

claim: For positive intensity levels, a one-point glider produces textures with increasingly large luminance.
source: For instance (see examples in Figure 1A, right), for positive intensity levels, a one-point glider produces textures with increasingly large luminance, a two-point glider produces oriented edges and a four-point glider produces rectangular blocks.
evidence: This describes the visual appearance of different texture types and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: For positive intensity levels, a two-point glider produces oriented edges.
source: For instance (see examples in Figure 1A, right), for positive intensity levels, a one-point glider produces textures with increasingly large luminance, a two-point glider produces oriented edges and a four-point glider produces rectangular blocks.
evidence: This describes the visual appearance of different texture types and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: For positive intensity levels, a four-point glider produces rectangular blocks.
source: For instance (see examples in Figure 1A, right), for positive intensity levels, a one-point glider produces textures with increasingly large luminance, a two-point glider produces oriented edges and a four-point glider produces rectangular blocks.
evidence: This describes the visual appearance of different texture types and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: A three-point glider produces L-shape patterns, either black or white depending on whether the intensity is negative or positive.
source: A three-point glider produces L-shape patterns, either black or white depending on whether the intensity is negative or positive.
evidence: This describes the visual appearance of three-point textures.

claim: Two-point and three-point gliders are associated to multiple distinct multipoint correlations, corresponding to different spatial glider configurations.
source: Notably, two-point and three-point gliders are associated to multiple distinct multipoint correlations, corresponding to different spatial glider configurations.
evidence: This describes a property of the texture statistics based on the method from Victor and Conte, 2012.

claim: In the previous study with human participants, all two-point, three-point, and four-point configurations were tested, as well as 11 of their pairwise combinations, for a total of 20 different texture statistics.
source: In our previous study with human participants (Hermundstad et al., 2014), we tested all these two-point, three-point, and four-point configurations, as well as 11 of their pairwise combinations, for a total of 20 different texture statistics.
evidence: This describes the scope of the previous human study with citation.

claim: Textures defined by one-point correlations were not tested in the previous human study because the method used to measure variability of texture statistics across natural images could not be applied to the one-point statistic.
source: In that set of experiments, we did not test textures defined by one-point correlations because, by construction, the method we used to measure the variability of texture statistics across natural images could not be applied to the one-point statistic.
evidence: This explains a methodological limitation of the previous study.

claim: Practical and ethical constraints prevented measuring rat sensitivity to a large number of statistic combinations because a different group of animals had to be trained with each tested statistic.
source: In our current study, practical and ethical constraints prevented us from measuring rat sensitivity to a large number of statistic combinations, because a different group of animals had to be trained with each tested statistic (see below), meaning that the number of rats required for the experiments increased rapidly with the number of statistics studied.
evidence: This explains the experimental design constraints of the current study.

claim: The 4-point statistic was chosen for testing in rats.
source: Therefore, we chose to test the 4-point statistic, as well as one each of the two-point and three-point statistics (those shown in Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental design choice.

claim: The one-point statistic was tested because rat visual system sensitivity to luminance changes is well-established and performance with this statistic served as a useful benchmark.
source: In addition, we also tested the one-point statistic because, given the well-established sensitivity of the rat visual system to luminance changes (Minini and Jeffery, 2006; Tafazoli et al., 2017; Vascon et al., 2019; Vermaercke and Op de Beeck, 2012), performance with this statistic served as a useful benchmark against which to compare rat discrimination of the other, more complex textures.
evidence: This explains the rationale for including one-point statistics with citations to previous work on rat vision.

claim: The rat visual system has well-established sensitivity to luminance changes.
source: In addition, we also tested the one-point statistic because, given the well-established sensitivity of the rat visual system to luminance changes (Minini and Jeffery, 2006; Tafazoli et al., 2017; Vascon et al., 2019; Vermaercke and Op de Beeck, 2012), performance with this statistic served as a useful benchmark against which to compare rat discrimination of the other, more complex textures.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies on rat vision.

claim: In Hermundstad et al., 2014, both positive and negative values of the statistics were probed against white noise.
source: Finally, while in Hermundstad et al., 2014, both positive and negative values of the statistics were probed against white noise, here we tested only one side of the texture intensity axis (either positive, for one-, two-, and four-point configurations, or negative, for three-point ones) — again, with the goal of limiting the number of rats used in the experiment (see Materials and methods for more details on the rationale behind the choice of statistics and their polarity, and see Discussion for an assessment of the possible impact of these choices on our conclusions).
evidence: This describes a difference in experimental design between the current and previous studies.

claim: In the current study, only one side of the texture intensity axis was tested (positive for one-, two-, and four-point configurations, or negative for three-point).
source: Finally, while in Hermundstad et al., 2014, both positive and negative values of the statistics were probed against white noise, here we tested only one side of the texture intensity axis (either positive, for one-, two-, and four-point configurations, or negative, for three-point ones) — again, with the goal of limiting the number of rats used in the experiment (see Materials and methods for more details on the rationale behind the choice of statistics and their polarity, and see Discussion for an assessment of the possible impact of these choices on our conclusions).
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the current study.

claim: Each trial started with the rat autonomously triggering stimulus presentation by licking the central response port.
source: Each trial of the experiment started with the rat autonomously triggering the presentation of a stimulus by licking the central response port within an array of three (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the behavioral task procedure illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The animal reported whether the texture contained the statistic by licking the left port or white noise by licking the right port.
source: The animal then reported whether the texture displayed over the monitor placed in front of him contained the statistic (by licking the left port) or white noise (by licking the right port).
evidence: This describes the behavioral task procedure.

claim: The rat received liquid reward for correct choices and was subjected to a time-out period for incorrect ones.
source: The rat received liquid reward for correct choices and was subjected to a time-out period for incorrect ones (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the reinforcement schedule used in the behavioral task.

claim: In the initial phase of the experiment, the intensity of the statistic was set to a single level close to the maximum (or minimum for three-point) to make discrimination as easy as possible for naive rats.
source: In the initial phase of the experiment, the intensity of the statistic was set to a single level, close to the maximum (or minimum, in case of the three-point statistic, for which we used only negative values), to make the discrimination between structured textures and white noise as easy as possible for naive rats that had to learn the task from scratch.
evidence: This describes the training procedure.

claim: Animals trained on one- and two-point statistics reached criterion performance earlier than those trained on three- and four-point statistics.
source: As exemplified by these four animals, rats trained on different statistics required different lengths of time to learn the discrimination – animals trained on one- and two-point statistics reached and maintained a performance above criterion considerably earlier than those trained on three- and four-point.
evidence: This is based on analysis of learning curves shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Animals trained on one-point correlations required on average 3.5 ± 0.3 blocks of 500 trials to reach criterion (n = 9).
source: Specifically, considering only those rats that reached criterion performance, animals trained on one-point correlations required on average 3.5 ± 0.3 blocks of 500 trials (n = 9) to reach criterion; those trained on two-point correlations 5.3 ± 1.3 (n = 8); those trained on 3-point statistic 3.4 ± 1.6 (n = 5); and those trained on four-point correlations 11.8 ± 1.6 (n = 10).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the learning phase of the experiment.

claim: Animals trained on two-point correlations required on average 5.3 ± 1.3 blocks of 500 trials to reach criterion (n = 8).
source: Specifically, considering only those rats that reached criterion performance, animals trained on one-point correlations required on average 3.5 ± 0.3 blocks of 500 trials (n = 9) to reach criterion; those trained on two-point correlations 5.3 ± 1.3 (n = 8); those trained on 3-point statistic 3.4 ± 1.6 (n = 5); and those trained on four-point correlations 11.8 ± 1.6 (n = 10).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the learning phase of the experiment.

claim: Animals trained on three-point correlations required on average 3.4 ± 1.6 blocks of 500 trials to reach criterion (n = 5).
source: Specifically, considering only those rats that reached criterion performance, animals trained on one-point correlations required on average 3.5 ± 0.3 blocks of 500 trials (n = 9) to reach criterion; those trained on two-point correlations 5.3 ± 1.3 (n = 8); those trained on 3-point statistic 3.4 ± 1.6 (n = 5); and those trained on four-point correlations 11.8 ± 1.6 (n = 10).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the learning phase of the experiment.

claim: Animals trained on four-point correlations required on average 11.8 ± 1.6 blocks of 500 trials to reach criterion (n = 10).
source: Specifically, considering only those rats that reached criterion performance, animals trained on one-point correlations required on average 3.5 ± 0.3 blocks of 500 trials (n = 9) to reach criterion; those trained on two-point correlations 5.3 ± 1.3 (n = 8); those trained on 3-point statistic 3.4 ± 1.6 (n = 5); and those trained on four-point correlations 11.8 ± 1.6 (n = 10).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the learning phase of the experiment.

claim: In the second phase of the experiment, the intensity of the statistic was gradually reduced using an adaptive staircase procedure to make the task progressively harder.
source: In the following phase of the experiment, the intensity of the statistic was gradually reduced using an adaptive staircase procedure (see Materials and methods) to make the task progressively harder.
evidence: This describes the training procedure.

claim: Following training, rats were subjected to a main testing phase where textures were sampled at regular intervals along the intensity level axis and randomly presented.
source: Following this training, rats were subjected to: (1) a main testing phase, where textures were sampled at regular intervals along the intensity level axis and were randomly presented to the animals; and (2) a further testing phase, where rats originally trained with a given statistic were probed with a different one (see Materials and methods for details on training and testing).
evidence: This describes the testing procedure.

claim: Rats were also subjected to a further testing phase where they were probed with a different statistic than the one they were originally trained on.
source: Following this training, rats were subjected to: (1) a main testing phase, where textures were sampled at regular intervals along the intensity level axis and were randomly presented to the animals; and (2) a further testing phase, where rats originally trained with a given statistic were probed with a different one (see Materials and methods for details on training and testing).
evidence: This describes the testing procedure for generalization.

claim: The main test phase yielded psychometric curves showing the sensitivity of each animal in discriminating white noise from the structured texture with the assigned statistic.
source: The main test phase yielded psychometric curves showing the sensitivity of each animal in discriminating white noise from the structured texture with the assigned statistic (example in Figure 2A, black dots).
evidence: This describes the data obtained from the main testing phase, illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: In the ideal observer model, σ measures the 'blurriness' in the animal's sensory representation for a particular type of statistic (the perceptual noise).
source: Here, σ measures the 'blurriness' in the animal's sensory representation for a particular type of statistic (i.e. the perceptual noise) and, consequently, its inverse 1/σ captures its resolution, or sensitivity — i.e., the perceptual threshold for discriminating a structured texture from white noise.
evidence: This explains the interpretation of a model parameter.

claim: The inverse of σ (1/σ) captures the animal's resolution or sensitivity, i.e., the perceptual threshold for discriminating a structured texture from white noise.
source: Here, σ measures the 'blurriness' in the animal's sensory representation for a particular type of statistic (i.e. the perceptual noise) and, consequently, its inverse 1/σ captures its resolution, or sensitivity — i.e., the perceptual threshold for discriminating a structured texture from white noise.
evidence: This explains the interpretation of a model parameter.

claim: Fitting the ideal observer model to behavioral data led to psychometric functions with a characteristic shape that depended on the order of the multipoint statistic an animal had to discriminate.
source: Fitting this model to the behavioral choices of rats in the four groups led to psychometric functions with a characteristic shape, which depended on the order of the multipoint statistic an animal had to discriminate (Figure 2B).
evidence: This describes the results of model fitting shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The sensitivity ranking for two-point horizontal, three-point, and four-point correlations in rats was the same as observed in humans and as the variability ranking measured across natural images.
source: When focusing on the texture statistics that had been also tested in our previous study (i.e. two-point horizontal, three-point, and four-point correlations), this sensitivity ranking was the same as the one observed in humans and as the variability ranking measured across natural images (Hermundstad et al., 2014): two-point horizontal > four-point > three-point.
evidence: This compares the current rat data to previous human data and natural image statistics.

claim: The sensitivity ranking for the tested statistics was: two-point horizontal > four-point > three-point.
source: When focusing on the texture statistics that had been also tested in our previous study (i.e. two-point horizontal, three-point, and four-point correlations), this sensitivity ranking was the same as the one observed in humans and as the variability ranking measured across natural images (Hermundstad et al., 2014): two-point horizontal > four-point > three-point.
evidence: This summarizes the main finding of the study.

claim: The actual values of rat sensitivity matched, up to a scaling factor, both human sensitivity and the standard deviation of the statistics in natural images.
source: Moreover, for the set of statistics that were studied both here and in Hermundstad et al., 2014, the actual values of the rat sensitivity matched, up to a scaling factor, both the human sensitivity and the standard deviation of the statistics in natural images (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison shown in Figure 3.

claim: The degree of correspondence between rat sensitivity and image statistics was 0.986 (p-value: 0.07).
source: The degree of correspondence was 0.986 between rat sensitivity and image statistics (p-value: 0.07, Monte Carlo test), and 0.990 between rat sensitivity and human sensitivity (p-value: 0.05, Monte Carlo test).
evidence: This is a quantitative statistical result from comparing rat sensitivity to natural image statistics.

claim: The degree of correspondence between rat sensitivity and human sensitivity was 0.990 (p-value: 0.05).
source: The degree of correspondence was 0.986 between rat sensitivity and image statistics (p-value: 0.07, Monte Carlo test), and 0.990 between rat sensitivity and human sensitivity (p-value: 0.05, Monte Carlo test).
evidence: This is a quantitative statistical result from comparing rat and human sensitivity.

claim: Hermundstad et al., 2014 reported values between 0.987 and 0.999 for the degree of correspondence between human sensitivity and image statistics.
source: For reference, Hermundstad et al., 2014 reported values between 0.987 and 0.999 for the degree of correspondence between human sensitivity and image statistics.
evidence: This is a reference value from the previous human study.

claim: There is not only a qualitative but also a quantitative agreement between rat findings and the pattern of texture sensitivity predicted by efficient coding.
source: This indicates not only a qualitative but also a quantitative agreement between our findings and the pattern of texture sensitivity predicted by efficient coding.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the degree of correspondence analysis.

claim: Rats trained on one- and two-point statistics performed poorly with higher-order correlations (three- and four-point).
source: Rats trained on one- and two-point statistics (the most discriminable ones; see Figure 2C) performed poorly with higher-order correlations (compare the green and purple star with the red star, and the green and purple cross with the blue cross in Figure 4), while animals trained on the four-point statistic performed on two-point correlations as well as rats that were originally trained on those textures (compare the blue square to the blue cross).
evidence: This describes results from the generalization testing phase shown in Figure 4.

claim: Animals trained on the four-point statistic performed on two-point correlations as well as rats that were originally trained on two-point textures.
source: Rats trained on one- and two-point statistics (the most discriminable ones; see Figure 2C) performed poorly with higher-order correlations (compare the green and purple star with the red star, and the green and purple cross with the blue cross in Figure 4), while animals trained on the four-point statistic performed on two-point correlations as well as rats that were originally trained on those textures (compare the blue square to the blue cross).
evidence: This describes results from the generalization testing phase shown in Figure 4.

claim: The better discriminability of textures containing lower order correlations is a robust phenomenon independent of training history and observable within individual subjects.
source: This shows that the better discriminability of textures containing lower order correlations is a robust phenomenon, which is independent of the history of training and observable within individual subjects.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the generalization testing results.

claim: Performance on four-point correlations was higher than performance on three-point correlations for each group of rats.
source: Moreover, performance on four-point correlations was higher than performance on three-point correlations for each group of rats (compare the green to the purple symbols connected by a line).
evidence: This describes a consistent pattern across groups shown in Figure 4.

claim: Rats trained on four-point and switching to three-point showed higher sensitivity to four-point than three-point (p < 0.01, paired one-tailed t-test).
source: This was true, in particular, not only for rats trained on four-point and switching to three-point (green vs. purple square, p < 0.01, paired one-tailed t-test) but even for rats trained on three-points and switching to four-point (green vs. purple triangle, p < 0.05, paired one-tailed t-test).
evidence: This is a statistical result from within-subject comparisons.

claim: Rats trained on three-point and switching to four-point showed higher sensitivity to four-point than three-point (p < 0.05, paired one-tailed t-test).
source: This was true, in particular, not only for rats trained on four-point and switching to three-point (green vs. purple square, p < 0.01, paired one-tailed t-test) but even for rats trained on three-points and switching to four-point (green vs. purple triangle, p < 0.05, paired one-tailed t-test).
evidence: This is a statistical result from within-subject comparisons.

claim: The larger discriminability of the four-point statistic compared to the three-point one is a statistically robust phenomenon within individual subjects.
source: This means that the larger discriminability of the four-point statistic, as compared to the three-point one, is a statistically robust phenomenon within individual subjects.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the within-subject statistical comparisons.

claim: Rat sensitivity to multipoint statistics is similar to that previously observed in humans and to the variability of multipoint correlations measured across natural images.
source: Overall, our results show that rat sensitivity to multipoint statistics is similar to the one we previously observed in humans and to the variability of multipoint correlations we previously measured across natural images (Hermundstad et al., 2014; Tkacik et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental results and comparisons to previous work.

claim: The agreement between rat sensitivity, human sensitivity, and natural image statistics holds both qualitatively and quantitatively.
source: This agreement holds both qualitatively and quantitatively (Figures 2—4).
evidence: This summarizes the main finding with reference to the figures showing the data.

claim: The expected sensitivity ranking (two-point horizontal > four-point > three-point) was found to be robust not only across groups but also for animals sequentially tested with multiple texture statistics.
source: Importantly, we found the expected sensitivity ranking (two-point horizontal > four-point > three-point) to be robust not only across groups (Figure 2C) but also for animals that were sequentially tested with multiple texture statistics (Figure 4) - and even at the within-subject level for the crucial three-point vs. four-point comparison.
evidence: This summarizes the robustness of the main finding across different analyses.

claim: The sensitivity ranking was robust at the within-subject level for the three-point vs. four-point comparison.
source: Importantly, we found the expected sensitivity ranking (two-point horizontal > four-point > three-point) to be robust not only across groups (Figure 2C) but also for animals that were sequentially tested with multiple texture statistics (Figure 4) - and even at the within-subject level for the crucial three-point vs. four-point comparison.
evidence: This highlights the robustness of a key finding.

claim: A high degree of correspondence was found between rat and human sensitivities.
source: Moreover, we found a high degree of correspondence between rat and human sensitivities (Figure 3).
evidence: This summarizes a quantitative comparison shown in Figure 3.

claim: The three texture statistics tested in both the present study and Hermundstad et al., 2014 are sufficient to allow a meaningful comparison between rat and human sensitivities.
source: We addressed this matter at the level of experimental design, by carefully choosing the three statistics that, based on the sensitivity ranking observed in humans, would have yielded the cleanest signature of efficient coding (Hermundstad et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a justification for the experimental design based on previous findings.

claim: The two statistics selected were maximally and minimally variable across natural images and yielded the largest and lowest sensitivities in humans: horizontal two-point correlations and one of the three-point correlations.
source: That is, we selected two statistics that were, respectively, maximally and minimally variable across natural images, and yielded the largest and lowest sensitivities in humans: horizontal two-point correlations and one of the three-point correlations.
evidence: This explains the rationale for stimulus selection based on previous human data.

claim: Human sensitivity to the four-point statistic and its variability across natural images is only slightly larger than for the three-point configurations.
source: Additionally, human sensitivity to this statistic, as well as its variability across natural images, is only slightly larger than for the three-point configurations.
evidence: This is a finding from the previous human study.

claim: Finding a reliable sensitivity difference between three-point and four-point textures for rats would provide strong evidence for matching texture sensitivity across the two species.
source: Therefore, finding a reliable sensitivity difference between three-point and four-point textures also for rats would have provided strong evidence for matching texture sensitivity across the two species.
evidence: This is a prediction about what would constitute strong evidence for the hypothesis.

claim: For one-point correlations, positive intensity values were chosen because they yield patterns that are brighter than white noise.
source: For one-point correlations we chose positive intensity values because they yield patterns that are brighter than white noise.
evidence: This explains a design choice.

claim: Rat V1 neurons are very sensitive to increases of luminance.
source: Since previous work from our group has shown that rat V1 neurons are very sensitive to increases of luminance (Tafazoli et al., 2017; Vascon et al., 2019), our choice ensured that one-point textures were highly distinguishable from white noise (as indeed observed in our data; see Figure 2B–C), which was the key requirement for our benchmark statistic.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work from the same group.

claim: The choice of positive intensity for one-point statistics ensured that one-point textures were highly distinguishable from white noise, which was the key requirement for the benchmark statistic.
source: Since previous work from our group has shown that rat V1 neurons are very sensitive to increases of luminance (Tafazoli et al., 2017; Vascon et al., 2019), our choice ensured that one-point textures were highly distinguishable from white noise (as indeed observed in our data; see Figure 2B–C), which was the key requirement for our benchmark statistic.
evidence: This explains the rationale for a design choice and notes that the expected result was observed.

claim: Rodent species have much lower visual acuity than humans.
source: For two-point and four-point statistics we also used positive intensity values — a choice dictated by the need of testing a rodent species that has much lower visual acuity than humans (Keller et al., 2000; Prusky et al., 2002; Zoccolan, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on rodent vision.

claim: Positive two-point and four-point correlations give rise to large features (thick oriented stripes and wide rectangular blocks made of multiple pixels with the same color).
source: Positive two-point and four-point correlations give rise to large features (thick oriented stripes and wide rectangular blocks made of multiple pixels with the same color), while negative intensities produce higher spatial frequency patterns, where color may change every other pixel (see Figure 2A in Hermundstad et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes properties of the stimuli with reference to a figure in a previous paper.

claim: Negative intensities of two-point and four-point statistics produce higher spatial frequency patterns where color may change every other pixel.
source: Positive two-point and four-point correlations give rise to large features (thick oriented stripes and wide rectangular blocks made of multiple pixels with the same color), while negative intensities produce higher spatial frequency patterns, where color may change every other pixel (see Figure 2A in Hermundstad et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes properties of the stimuli with reference to a figure in a previous paper.

claim: Using negative two-point and four-point statistics would have introduced a possible confound, since low sensitivity could have been due to the low spatial resolution of rat vision.
source: Therefore, using negative two-point and four-point statistics would have introduced a possible confound, since low sensitivity to these textures could have been simply due to the low spatial resolution of rat vision.
evidence: This is an inference about a potential confound in experimental design.

claim: For three-point correlations, polarity does not affect the shape and size of the emerging visual patterns, but it determines their contrast.
source: For three-point correlations, polarity does not affect the shape and size of the emerging visual patterns, but it determines their contrast.
evidence: This describes a property of three-point textures.

claim: Positive and negative intensities of three-point statistics yield L-shaped patches that are, respectively, white and black.
source: Positive and negative intensities yield L-shaped patches that are, respectively, white and black.
evidence: This describes a property of three-point textures.

claim: Negative intensity values for three-point statistics were chosen to ensure that the well-known dominance of OFF responses would not play in favor of finding the lowest sensitivity for the three-point statistic.
source: In this case, we chose the latter to make sure that the well-known dominance of OFF responses observed across the visual systems of many mammal species would not play in favor of finding the lowest sensitivity for the three-point statistic.
evidence: This explains the rationale for a design choice based on known properties of visual systems.

claim: Primary visual neurons of primates and cats respond more strongly to black than to white spots and oriented bars.
source: In fact, several studies have shown that primary visual neurons of primates and cats respond more strongly to black than to white spots and oriented bars (Liu and Yao, 2014; Xing et al., 2010; Yeh et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to neurophysiology studies.

claim: The dominance of OFF responses over ON responses is observed in the central visual field of mice, although in the periphery OFF and ON responses are more balanced.
source: A very recent study has shown that this is the case also for the central visual field of mice, although in the periphery OFF and ON response are more balanced (Williams et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study on mouse vision.

claim: The asymmetry in OFF vs ON responses begins already in the retina where there are more OFF cells than ON cells.
source: Indeed, the asymmetry begins already in the retina where there are more OFF cells than ON cells (Ratliff et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on retinal cell populations.

claim: In the behavioral rigs, rats face frontally the stimulus display and maintain their head oriented frontally during stimulus presentation.
source: Since in our behavioral rigs rats face frontally the stimulus display (Figure 1B) and maintain their head oriented frontally during stimulus presentation (Vanzella et al., 2019), it was important that the L-shaped patterns produced by three-point correlations had the highest saliency.
evidence: This describes the behavioral setup with citation to a previous study.

claim: Choosing negative intensity values for three-point statistics ensured that L-shaped patterns had the highest saliency, excluding the possibility that low sensitivity was partially due to presentation at suboptimal contrast.
source: Choosing negative intensity values ensured that this was the case, thus excluding the possibility that the low-sensitivity found for three-point textures (Figures 2—4) was partially due to presentation at a suboptimal contrast.
evidence: This explains the rationale for a design choice and its implications for interpreting the results.

claim: Previous studies found human sensitivity to be nearly identical for negative and positive intensity variations of each of the statistics tested (one-point, two-point, three-point, and four-point correlations).
source: Previous studies, however, found human sensitivity to be nearly identical for negative and positive intensity variations of each of the statistic tested in our study: one-point, two-point, three-point, and four-point correlations (Victor and Conte, 2012), even in the face of asymmetries of the distribution of the corresponding statistic in natural images (see Figure 3—figure supplement 9 in Hermundstad et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous human psychophysics studies.

claim: The choices of texture types and their polarity were dictated by the need to adapt to a rodent species texture stimuli that have only been used in psychophysics studies with humans and neurophysiology studies in monkeys.
source: In summary, our choices of texture types and their polarity were all dictated by the need of adapting to a rodent species texture stimuli that, so far, have only been used in psychophysics studies with humans (Hermundstad et al., 2014; Tesileanu et al., 2020; Tkacik et al., 2010; Victor and Conte, 2012) and neurophysiology studies in monkeys (Purpura et al., 1994; Yu et al., 2015).
evidence: This summarizes the rationale for experimental design choices with citations to previous work.

claim: The goal of the experimental design was to maximize the sensitivity of the comparison with humans and natural image statistics while reducing the possible impact of confounding factors.
source: Our goal was to maximize the sensitivity of the comparison with humans and natural image statistics, while reducing the possible impact of phenomena (such as rat low visual acuity and the dominance of OFF responses) that could have acted as confounding factors.
evidence: This explains the overall strategy for experimental design.

claim: The findings provide a robust demonstration that a rodent species and humans are similarly adapted to process the statistical structure of visual textures in a way consistent with the computational principle of efficient coding.
source: Thanks to these measures, our findings provide a robust demonstration that a rodent species and humans are similarly adapted to process the statistical structure of visual textures, in a way that is consistent with the computational principle of efficient coding.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The findings attest to the fundamental role of natural image statistics in shaping visual processing across species.
source: This attests to the fundamental role of natural image statistics in shaping visual processing across species, and opens a path toward a causal test of efficient coding through the altered-rearing experiments that small mammals, such as rodents, allow (Hunt et al., 2013; Matteucci and Zoccolan, 2020; White and Fitzpatrick, 2007).
evidence: This is an inference about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: The findings open a path toward a causal test of efficient coding through altered-rearing experiments that small mammals allow.
source: This attests to the fundamental role of natural image statistics in shaping visual processing across species, and opens a path toward a causal test of efficient coding through the altered-rearing experiments that small mammals, such as rodents, allow (Hunt et al., 2013; Matteucci and Zoccolan, 2020; White and Fitzpatrick, 2007).
evidence: This is an inference about future research directions enabled by the current findings, with citations to relevant work.

claim: A total of 42 male adult Long Evans rats were tested in a visual texture discrimination task.
source: A total of 42 male adult Long Evans rats (Charles River Laboratories) were tested in a visual texture discrimination task.
evidence: This describes the subjects used in the study.

claim: Animals started training at 10 weeks, after 1 week of quarantine and 2 weeks of handling.
source: Animals started the training at 10 weeks, after 1 week of quarantine upon arrival in our institute and 2 weeks of handling to familiarize them with the experimenters.
evidence: This describes the experimental timeline and procedures.

claim: Rats' weight at arrival was approximately 300 g and they grew to over 600 g over the time span of the experiment.
source: Their weight at arrival was approximately 300 g and they grew to over 600 g over the time span of the experiment.
evidence: This provides descriptive information about the subjects.

claim: Rats always had free access to food but their access to water was restricted in the days of behavioral training (5 days a week).
source: Rats always had free access to food but their access to water was restricted in the days of the behavioral training (5 days a week).
evidence: This describes the husbandry and motivation procedures.

claim: Rats received 10–20 ml of diluted pear juice (1:4) during execution of the discrimination task.
source: They received 10–20 ml of diluted pear juice (1:4) during the execution of the discrimination task, after which they were also given free access to water for the time needed to reach at least the recommended 50 ml/kg intake per day.
evidence: This describes the reward and hydration procedures.

claim: The number of rats was chosen to yield meaningful statistical analyses (about 10 subjects per texture statistic) under the capacity constraint of the behavioral rig.
source: The number of rats was chosen in such a way to yield meaningful statistical analyses (i.e. to have about 10 subjects for each of the texture statistic tested in our study), under the capacity constraint of our behavioral rig.
evidence: This explains the rationale for sample size.

claim: The behavioral rig allows simultaneous testing of six rats during 1–1.5 hr.
source: The rig allows to simultaneously test six rats, during the course of 1–1.5 hr (Zoccolan, 2015; Djurdjevic et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the experimental setup with citations to previous work.

claim: The first batch of 24 animals (6 per statistic) arrived in November 2018 and was tested throughout most of 2019.
source: The first batch arrived in November 2018 and was tested throughout most of 2019; the second group arrived in September 2019 and was tested throughout most of 2020.
evidence: This provides timeline information for the experiments.

claim: The second batch of 18 animals arrived in September 2019 and was tested throughout most of 2020.
source: The first batch arrived in November 2018 and was tested throughout most of 2019; the second group arrived in September 2019 and was tested throughout most of 2020.
evidence: This provides timeline information for the experiments.

claim: In the first batch, four animals did not reach the test phase because three did not achieve criterion performance and one died shortly after the beginning of the study.
source: In the first batch, four animals did not reach the test phase (i.e. the phase yielding the data shown in Figure 2A and B), because three of them did not achieve the criterion performance during the initial training phase (see below) and one died shortly after the beginning of the study.
evidence: This describes attrition in the first batch of subjects.

claim: In the second batch, one rat died before reaching the test phase and two more died before the last test phase with switched statistics.
source: In the second batch, one rat died before reaching the test phase and two more died before the last test phase with switched statistics (i.e. the phase yielding the data of Figure 2C).
evidence: This describes attrition in the second batch of subjects.

claim: All animal procedures were conducted in accordance with international and institutional standards and were approved by the Italian Ministry of Health.
source: All animal procedures were conducted in accordance with the international and institutional standards for the care and use of animals in research and were approved by the Italian Ministry of Health and after consulting with a veterinarian (Project DGSAF 25271, submitted on December 1, 2014 and approved on September 4, 2015, approval 940/2015-PR).
evidence: This describes ethical approval for the study.

claim: Each operant box was equipped with a 21.5" LCD monitor (ASUS VEZZHR) for presentation of visual stimuli.
source: Each box was equipped with a 21.5" LCD monitor (ASUS VEZZHR) for the presentation of the visual stimuli and an array of three stainless-steel feeding needles (Cadence Science), serving as response ports.
evidence: This describes the experimental apparatus.

claim: Each texture had a size of 39 × 22 pixels and occupied the entire monitor (full-field stimuli).
source: Each texture had a size of 39 × 22 pixels and occupied the entire monitor (full-field stimuli).
evidence: This describes the stimulus properties.

claim: The pixels had a dimension of about 2 degrees of visual angle.
source: The pixels had a dimension of about 2 degrees of visual angle.
evidence: This describes the stimulus properties in terms of visual angle.

claim: The maximal resolution of rat vision is about one cycle per degree.
source: Given that the maximal resolution of rat vision is about one cycle per degree (Keller et al., 2000; Prusky et al., 2000; Prusky et al., 2002), such a choice of the pixel size guaranteed that the animals could discriminate between neighboring pixels of different color.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on rat visual acuity.

claim: The choice of pixel size (about 2 degrees of visual angle) guaranteed that the animals could discriminate between neighboring pixels of different color.
source: Given that the maximal resolution of rat vision is about one cycle per degree (Keller et al., 2000; Prusky et al., 2000; Prusky et al., 2002), such a choice of the pixel size guaranteed that the animals could discriminate between neighboring pixels of different color.
evidence: This is an inference about stimulus design based on known properties of rat vision.

claim: The LCD monitors were calibrated to have minimal luminance of 0.126 ± 0.004 cd/mm (average ± SD across six monitors).
source: Textures were showed at full-contrast over the LCD monitors that were calibrated in such a way to have minimal luminance of 0.126 ± 0.004 cd/mm (average ± SD across the six monitors), maximal luminance of 129 ± 5 cd/mm, and an approximately linear luminance response curve.
evidence: This describes the calibration of the display equipment.

claim: The LCD monitors were calibrated to have maximal luminance of 129 ± 5 cd/mm.
source: Textures were showed at full-contrast over the LCD monitors that were calibrated in such a way to have minimal luminance of 0.126 ± 0.004 cd/mm (average ± SD across the six monitors), maximal luminance of 129 ± 5 cd/mm, and an approximately linear luminance response curve.
evidence: This describes the calibration of the display equipment.

claim: The LCD monitors had an approximately linear luminance response curve.
source: Textures were showed at full-contrast over the LCD monitors that were calibrated in such a way to have minimal luminance of 0.126 ± 0.004 cd/mm (average ± SD across the six monitors), maximal luminance of 129 ± 5 cd/mm, and an approximately linear luminance response curve.
evidence: This describes the calibration of the display equipment.

claim: The stimulus remained on the display until the animal responded or for a maximum of 5 s, after which the trial was considered as ignored.
source: The stimulus remained on the display until the animal responded or for a maximum of 5 s, after which the trial was considered as ignored.
evidence: This describes the trial structure.

claim: In case of a correct response, the stimulus was removed, a positive reinforcement sound was played, and a white or gray background was shown during delivery of the reward.
source: In case of a correct response the stimulus was removed, a positive reinforcement sound was played and a white (first animal batch) or gray (second batch) background was shown during delivery of the reward.
evidence: This describes the feedback for correct responses.

claim: In case of an incorrect choice, the stimulus was removed and a 1–3 s time-out period started during which the screen flickered from middle-gray to black at 10 Hz while a 'failure' sound was played.
source: In case of an incorrect choice, the stimulus was removed and a 1–3 s time-out period started, during which the screen flickered from middle-gray to black at a rate of 10 Hz, while a 'failure' sound was played.
evidence: This describes the feedback for incorrect responses.

claim: Trials where animals responded in less than 300 or 400 ms were considered as aborted.
source: To prevent the rats from making impulsive random choices, trials where the animals responded in less than 300 or 400 ms were considered as aborted: the stimulus was immediately removed and a brief sound was played.
evidence: This describes a rule to prevent impulsive responding.

claim: In each trial, visual stimuli had the same probability (50%) of being sampled from the pool of white noise textures or from the pool of structured textures.
source: In each trial, the visual stimuli had the same probability (50%) of being sampled from the pool of white noise textures or from the pool of structured textures, with the constraint that stimuli belonging to the same category were shown for at most n consecutive trials (with n varying between 2 and 3 depending on the animal and on the session), so as to prevent the rats from developing a bias toward one of the response ports.
evidence: This describes the stimulus presentation schedule.

claim: Stimuli belonging to the same category were shown for at most 2-3 consecutive trials to prevent rats from developing a bias toward one response port.
source: In each trial, the visual stimuli had the same probability (50%) of being sampled from the pool of white noise textures or from the pool of structured textures, with the constraint that stimuli belonging to the same category were shown for at most n consecutive trials (with n varying between 2 and 3 depending on the animal and on the session), so as to prevent the rats from developing a bias toward one of the response ports.
evidence: This describes a constraint on stimulus presentation to prevent response bias.

claim: Stimulus presentation, response collection and reward delivery were controlled via workstations running the open source suite MWorks.
source: Stimulus presentation, response collection and reward delivery were controlled via workstations running the open source suite MWorks (https://mworks.github.io;Starwarz and Cox, 2021).
evidence: This describes the software used for experimental control.

claim: Out of 42 rats, 9 were trained with one-point statistics, 9 with two-point, 12 with three-point, and 12 with four-point.
source: Out of the 42 rats, 9 were trained with one-point statistics, 9 with two-point, 12 with three-point, and 12 with four-point.
evidence: This describes the distribution of subjects across experimental conditions.

claim: The animals that reached phase III were 9, 9, 8, and 11, respectively, for the four statistics.
source: The animals that reached phase III were 9, 9, 8, and 11, respectively, for the four statistics.
evidence: This describes the number of subjects that completed training for each condition.

claim: In Phase I, rats were trained to discriminate white noise from structured textures containing a single high-intensity level (0.85 for one- and two-point; 0.95 for three- and four-point).
source: Initially, rats were trained to discriminate unstructured textures made of white noise from structured textures containing a single high-intensity level of one of the statistics (for one-point and two-point: 0.85; for three-point and four-point: 0.95).
evidence: This describes the initial training procedure.

claim: In each trial of Phase I, both kinds of stimuli were randomly sampled without replacement from a pool of 350 different textures.
source: To make sure that the animals learned a general distinction between structured and unstructured textures (and not between specific instances of the two stimulus categories), in each trial both kinds of stimuli were randomly sampled (without replacement) from a pool of 350 different textures.
evidence: This describes the stimulus sampling procedure to ensure generalization.

claim: Since rats typically performed 200-300 trials in a training session, every single texture was not shown more than once per session.
source: Since the rats typically performed between 200 and 300 trials in a training session, every single texture was not shown more than once.
evidence: This is an inference about stimulus repetition based on the pool size and typical trial counts.

claim: A different pool of textures was used in each of the five days within a week of training, and the same five pools were reused the following week.
source: A different pool of textures was used in each of the five days within a week of training. The same five texture pools were then used again (in the same order) the following week.
evidence: This describes the stimulus rotation schedule.

claim: At least 7 days had to pass before a given texture stimulus was presented again to a rat.
source: Therefore, at least 7 days had to pass before a given texture stimulus was presented again to a rat.
evidence: This is an inference about the minimum interval between stimulus repetitions based on the rotation schedule.

claim: For the first batch of rats, animals that reached at least 65% correct choices over 500 trials were moved to the second phase.
source: For the first batch of rats, we moved to the second phase of the experiment all the animals that were able to reach at least an average performance of 65% correct choices over a set of 500 trials, collected across a variable number of consecutive sessions (the learning curves of four example rats from this batch, one per group, are shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the criterion for advancing to the next phase for the first batch.

claim: Based on the 65% criterion, two rats tested with three-point textures and one rat tested with four-point textures were excluded from further testing in the first batch.
source: Based on this criterion, two rats tested with three-point textures and one rat tested with four-point textures were excluded from further testing.
evidence: This describes which animals did not meet the criterion in the first batch.

claim: For the second batch of rats, all animals were admitted to the following experimental phases after a prolonged period of training in the first phase.
source: For the second batch of rats, we decided to admit all the animals to the following experimental phases after a prolonged period of training in the first phase.
evidence: This describes a different criterion for the second batch.

claim: Imposing a criterion performance in the first phase could bias the pool of rats tested with very difficult statistics toward including only exceptionally proficient animals, potentially overestimating typical rat sensitivity.
source: In fact, we reasoned that, in case some texture statistic was particularly hard to discriminate, imposing a criterion performance in the first phase of the experiment would bias the pool of rats tested with such very difficult statistic toward including only exceptionally proficient animals. This in turn, could lead to an overestimation of rat typical sensitivity to such difficult statistic.
evidence: This explains the reasoning for not using a criterion in the second batch.

claim: Failure to reach criterion performance could be due to intrinsic limitations of a rat's visual apparatus such as a malfunctioning retina or particularly low acuity.
source: On the other hand, the failure of a rat to reach a given criterion performance could be due to intrinsic limitations of its visual apparatus (such as a malfunctioning retina or particularly low acuity).
evidence: This is speculation about possible reasons for poor performance.

claim: Perceptual sensitivities were re-estimated after excluding rats from the second batch that did not reach 65% correct discrimination in the first training phase, and the resulting sensitivity ranking was unchanged.
source: Therefore, to make sure that our result did not depend on including in our analysis some animals of the second batch that did not reach 65% correct discrimination in the first training phase, the perceptual sensitivities were re-estimated after excluding those rats (i.e. after excluding one rat from the two-point, three rats from the three-point, and one from the four-point groups). As shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, the resulting sensitivity ranking was unchanged (compare to Figure 2C) and all pairwise comparisons remained statistically significant (two-sample t-test with Holm-Bonferroni correction).
evidence: This describes a control analysis and its results.

claim: In Phase II, progressively lower levels of intensity of each statistic were introduced, bringing them gradually closer to the zero-intensity level corresponding to white noise.
source: In this phase, we introduced progressively lower levels of intensity of each statistic, bringing them gradually closer to the zero-intensity level corresponding to white noise.
evidence: This describes the procedure for Phase II.

claim: An adaptive staircase procedure was applied to update the minimum level of the statistic based on the rat's current performance.
source: To this end, we applied an adaptive staircase procedure to update the minimum level of the statistic to be presented to a rat based on its current performance.
evidence: This describes the adaptive procedure used in Phase II.

claim: In any given trial of Phase II, the level of the multipoint correlation in structured textures was randomly sampled between a minimum level (controlled by the staircase) and a maximum level (fixed at the Phase I value).
source: Briefly, in any given trial, the level of the multipoint correlation in the structured textures was randomly sampled between a minimum level (under the control of the staircase procedure) and a maximum level (fixed at the value used in phase I).
evidence: This describes the stimulus sampling procedure in Phase II.

claim: Within the range of intensity levels in Phase II, sampling was not uniform but used a geometric distribution with peak at the minimum level.
source: Within this range, the sampling was not uniform, but was carried out using a geometric distribution (with the peak at the minimum level), so as to make much more likely for rats to be presented with intensity levels at or close to the minimum.
evidence: This describes the sampling distribution used in Phase II.

claim: Performance on the current minimum intensity level was computed every ten trials in Phase II.
source: The performance achieved by the rats on the current minimum intensity level was computed every ten trials.
evidence: This describes the performance monitoring procedure.

claim: If performance was higher than 70% correct, the minimum intensity level was decreased by 0.05.
source: If such a performance was higher than 70% correct, the minimum intensity level was decreased by a step of 0.05.
evidence: This describes the staircase rule for decreasing difficulty.

claim: If performance was lower than 50%, the minimum intensity level was increased by 0.05.
source: By contrast, if the performance was lower than 50%, the minimum intensity level was increased of the same amount.
evidence: This describes the staircase rule for increasing difficulty.

claim: At the end of Phase II, the minimum intensity level reached was 0.21 ± 0.12 for one-point, 0.2 ± 0.2 for two-point, 0.70 ± 0.22 for three-point, and 0.56 ± 0.18 for four-point correlations (group average ± SD).
source: At the end of this phase, the minimum intensity level reached by the animal in the three groups was: 0.21 ± 0.12, 0.2 ± 0.2, 0.70 ± 0.22, and 0.56 ± 0.18 (group average ± SD) for, respectively, one-, two-, three-, and four-point correlations.
evidence: This provides quantitative results from Phase II training.

claim: In Phase III, the stimulus was either white noise or a patterned texture with equal probability.
source: In each trial of this phase, the stimulus was either white noise or a patterned texture with equal probability.
evidence: This describes the stimulus presentation in Phase III.

claim: If the stimulus was a patterned texture in Phase III, the level of the statistic was randomly selected from the set {0.02, 0.09, 0.16, …, 0.93, 1} with uniform probability.
source: If it was a patterned texture, the level of the statistic was randomly selected from the set {0.02, 0.09, 0.16, …, 0.93, 1} (i.e. from 0.02 to 1 in steps of 0.07) with uniform probability.
evidence: This describes the intensity levels tested in Phase III.

claim: Rat sensitivity was measured by fitting the Bayesian ideal observer model to the psychometric curves from Phase III.
source: The responses of each rat over this range of intensity levels yielded psychometric curves (see example in Figure 1B), from which rat sensitivity was measured by fitting the Bayesian ideal observer model described below (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This describes the analysis method for Phase III data.

claim: In Phase IV, each rat was tested on a new statistic different from the one the animal was previously trained and tested on.
source: To verify the sensitivity ranking observed in phase III, we carried out an additional test phase, where each rat was tested on a new statistic, which was different from the one the animal was previously trained and tested on.
evidence: This describes the purpose and design of Phase IV.

claim: The two groups of rats originally trained with one- and two-point statistics were split into subgroups and each subgroup was tested with three- and four-point correlations.
source: The two groups of rats that were originally trained with the statistics yielding the highest sensitivity in phase III (i.e. one- and two-point correlations; see Figure 2B) were split in approximately equally-sized subgroups and each of these subgroups was tested with the less discriminable statistics (i.e. three- and four-point correlations; leftmost half of Figure 2C).
evidence: This describes the design of Phase IV for the one- and two-point groups.

claim: Rats originally tested with the three-point statistic were all switched to the four-point statistic in Phase IV.
source: For the group of rats originally tested with the three-point statistic, all the animals were switched to the four-point (third set of points in Figure 2C).
evidence: This describes the design of Phase IV for the three-point group.

claim: Most rats (8/11) originally trained/tested with four-point correlations were switched to the three-point statistic in Phase IV.
source: For the same reason, most of the rats (8/11) of the last group (i.e. the animals originally trained/tested with the four-point correlations; last set of points in Figure 2C) were switched to the three-point statistic, which yielded again the lowest discriminability.
evidence: This describes the design of Phase IV for most of the four-point group.

claim: A few animals (3/11) from the four-point group were tested with the two-point statistic in Phase IV.
source: A few animals (3/11) were instead tested with the two-point statistic, thus verifying that the latter was much more discriminable than the four-point one (again, despite the extensive training the animals of this group had received with the four-point textures).
evidence: This describes the design of Phase IV for a subset of the four-point group.
